summary: Geoffrey Barstow is a scholar of Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies. He studied at Hampshire College, Kathmandu University, the University of Virginia, and under Chökyi Nyima Rinpoche. He held posts at Virginia (~2013) and Oregon State University (~2013).

Geoffrey Goble works in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies. He earned an MA at the University of Virginia and a PhD at Indiana University Bloomington, and became Assistant Professor of Religious Studies at the University of Oklahoma in 2016.

Geoffrey Samuel is a scholar of religious studies, Tibetology, and Indology. Educated at Oxford and Cambridge under Edmund Leach, Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah, and Peter J. Wilson, he held positions at Newcastle (1978–2004), Lancaster (attested 1996), and Cardiff (attested 2008, 2014).

Georg August Wallin (1811–1852) was a scholar in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Katedralskolan i Åbo and the University of Helsinki (~1829–1836), where he later held a post from ~1851 to 1852.

Georg Buddruss (1929–2021) specialized in Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Goethe University Frankfurt under Paul Thieme and at the University of Tübingen, later serving as professor at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz from 1963 to 1995.

Georg Bühler (1837–1898) worked in Indology, linguistics, and archaeology. Educated under Ahrens, Kühner, and Benfey at Göttingen, he taught at Elphinstone College, University of Mumbai, and Deccan College (1863–1880), before taking a chair at the University of Vienna in 1880.

Georg Christoph Lichtenberg (1742–1799) worked in philosophy and other fields. He studied at the University of Göttingen (~1763–1767) and subsequently held an academic post there from ~1769 until 1799.

Georg Curtius (1820–1885) was a linguist who studied at Bonn and Berlin under Lassen, Ritschl, and Bopp. Following habilitation at Berlin, he served as professor at the University of Leipzig from 1862 to 1885.

Georg Ebers (1837–1898) worked in history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at Göttingen, Berlin under Lepsius and Boeckh, and Jena, later holding posts at the University of Jena (1869–1870) and the University of Leipzig (1870–1889).

Georg Forster (1754–1794) was an Indologist and natural historian who studied at Saint Peter's School. He held professorships at Collegium Carolinum (1779) and Vilnius University (1784–1787), and worked at Mainz University Library and Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (~1788–1793).

Georg Freytag (1788–1861) was a linguist who studied at Göttingen (~1807–1811) and under Silvestre de Sacy in Paris. He held posts at Göttingen (1811–1813), Königsberg (~1814–1815), and served as professor of oriental languages at Bonn (1819–1861).

Georg Friedrich Grotefend (1775–1853) was a linguist and Central Asian specialist. He studied under Heyne, Tychsen, and Heeren at Göttingen (1795). He taught at Max-Planck-Gymnasium Göttingen (1797), Lessing-Gymnasium (1803), and directed Ratsgymnasium Hannover from 1821 to 1849.
Georg Grimm (1868–1945) was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy. He lectured on Buddhism at the University of Munich and founded the Altbuddhistische Gemeinde in 1921.

Georg Heinrich Bernstein (1787–1860) worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Jena, Leipzig, Göttingen, and under Franz Bopp. He held posts at the University of Jena (1811), Humboldt University of Berlin (1812), and University of Breslau (1820).

Georg Heinrich Ferdinand Nesselmann (1811–1881) was a scholar of linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He earned his Ph.D. at Königsberg under Peter von Bohlen, serving there as PD (1838), ao. Professor (1843), and ordinary professor (1859).

Georg Huth (1867–1906) was an Indologist and Tibetologist. He studied at Berlin, Kiel, and Leipzig under Windisch, Oldenberg, and Deussen. He served as Privatdozent at Berlin (1891) and held a post at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin (~1892–1906).

Georg Jacob (1862–1937) was a historian who studied at Erlangen-Nuremberg, Strasbourg, Breslau, Berlin, and Leipzig under Fleischer, Nöldeke, and Spiegel. He held posts at Greifswald, Halle-Wittenberg, Erlangen-Nuremberg (1901–1909), and Kiel University (1911–1929).

Georg Kaibel (1849–1901) was a scholar in linguistics and history and archaeology. During his academic career, he held positions at the universities of Greifswald (~1879–1882), Breslau (~1882–1883), Rostock (~1883–1897), and Göttingen (~1897–1901).

Georg Ludolf Dissen (1784–1837) was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He studied at the University of Göttingen (~1804–1807), later holding academic posts at the University of Marburg (~1812–1813) and Göttingen (~1813–1837).

Georg Martin Dursch (1800–1881) was an Indologist and religious studies scholar. He completed doctoral studies at Tübingen (~1819–1825), studied Sanskrit under Antoine-Léonard Chézy in Paris (~1826–1829), and became a professor at Johann-Vanotti-Gymnasium Ehingen in 1828.
